sentences.text: Caulkicephalus is a genus of reptile belonging to the anhanguerid pterosaurs, a group of flying dinosaurs found on the Isle of Wight off the coast of England.
The preserved fossil material consists of snout fragments with a combined length of 290 millimeters.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — comprises three roughly contiguous pieces from the front of the snout.
A crest runs along the top of the snout, but it does not end in a rounded tip.
A damaged fragment from the back of the skull reveals the base of a parietal crest that likely pointed backward.

The teeth grew larger until the third pair, which were the longest, before the fourth pair matched the first in size, while the fifth, sixth, and seventh pairs became notably smaller, less than half the size of the earlier ones.
The genus name combines 'Caulkhead', a traditional nickname for Wight island residents, with the Greek word kephale meaning 'head', while the species name trimicrodon means 'three small teeth'.
David Martill estimated that this creature had a wingspan of nearly five meters.
Bone fragments of an unknown pterosaur were discovered between 1995 and 2003 at the Yaverland locality near Sandown.
The genus Caulkicephalus was named and described in 2005 by Lorna Steel, David Martill, David Unwin, and John Winch.
A constriction in the snout with larger teeth at the broad end, known as a 'prey grab', is interpreted as an adaptation for catching slippery prey like fish.
The presence of land plant debris in the fossil layer suggests Caulkicephalus may have inhabited a more terrestrial environment.
The type species of the genus Caulkicephalus is Caulkicephalus trimicrodon.
Studies in 2019 reassigned Caulkicephalus to the family Anhangueridae, subfamily Anhanguerinae, as a sister taxon to Guidraco and Ludodactylus.
Caulkicephalus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Barremian, from approximately 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago.
The fossils were found in brown clay from the Wessex Formation of the Wealden Group, dating to the Early Cretaceous (Barremian), approximately 130 million years ago.

The original describers assigned Caulkicephalus to the family Ornithocheiridae based on the narrowing in the middle of the snout, a classification later revised. The snout crest indicated membership in the broader group Ornithocheiroidea, while the parietal crest was suggested as a shared trait of the narrower group Euornithocheira. The parent group for Caulkicephalus is Ornithocheiridae.
